content: The medication bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide is typically administered as one tablet taken orally once daily. Bictegravir can increase the levels or effects of dofetilide by reducing its renal clearance, making their co-administration contraindicated. Bictegravir inhibits organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion transporter 1 (MATE1) in vitro, which may elevate plasma concentrations of drugs that are substrates of these transporters. Rifampin decreases the levels or effects of bictegravir by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism, and their co-administration is contraindicated. Strong inducers of CYP3A and UGT1A1 enzymes can significantly reduce bictegravir plasma concentrations, potentially leading to therapeutic failure and resistance development. Similarly, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, rifabutin, rifapentine, and St. John’s Wort also reduce bictegravir levels through CYP3A4 induction, and alternative drugs should be considered. Antiretroviral medications, including bictegravir, may interfere with the manufacturing of autologous cell therapies such as atidarsagene autotemcel, betibeglogene autotemcel, and lovotibeglogene autotemcel. Patients should discontinue antiretroviral therapy at least one month before cell mobilization and until all apheresis cycles are completed. Aluminum hydroxide, magnesium carbonate, calcium acetate, calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, magnesium citrate, magnesium gluconate, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium oxide, magnesium sulfate, and other polyvalent cation-containing agents can reduce bictegravir absorption in the gastrointestinal tract. Bictegravir should be taken on an empty stomach at least two hours before or six hours after these agents. However, bictegravir and calcium or iron supplements can be taken together with food. Certain drugs, such as leniolisib, enasidenib, darolutamide, encorafenib, fostamatinib, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, regorafenib, safinamide, tafamidis, tafamidis meglumine, and tucatinib, may increase the levels or effects of tenofovir alafenamide by inhibiting transporters like BCRP or P-glycoprotein (P-gp). Close monitoring for toxicities and dose adjustments of tenofovir or the interacting drug may be necessary. Drugs like orlistat may reduce the absorption of tenofovir alafenamide, potentially leading to virologic failure in HIV-infected patients. Frequent monitoring of HIV RNA levels is recommended, and orlistat should be discontinued if viral load increases. Bictegravir can increase metformin levels by inhibiting renal clearance through OCT2 and MATE1 transporters. Metformin dose adjustments may be required. Bictegravir may also increase the levels of co-administered drugs like metformin by similar mechanisms. Tenofovir alafenamide may increase the toxicity of drugs like cabozantinib, momelotinib, and voclosporin due to transporter interactions or nephrotoxicity. Monitoring for adverse effects and dose adjustments are recommended. Multivitamins and supplements containing iron or zinc can reduce bictegravir absorption. Bictegravir should be taken on an empty stomach at least two hours before or six hours after these supplements, unless taken with food. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir can increase the levels of both bictegravir and tenofovir alafenamide by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism.
